alabama.rufada_status: Alabama has adopted RUFADAA as the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, Act 2017-316 (HB 138), effective January 1, 2018, codified at Ala. Code §§ 19-1A-1 through 19-1A-18.
alabama.custodian_access: A fiduciary (personal representative, trustee, agent under a power of attorney, or conservator) can get the catalogue of electronic communications and other digital assets on a lighter showing, but the content of electronic communications only with the user's consent or a court order. The custodian may choose how to disclose: full account access, partial access, or a copy of the assets. It may demand a written request, a certified death certificate, proof of appointment such as letters testamentary, and the will, trust, or power of attorney showing consent, and it must comply within 60 days of a valid request.
alabama.user_direction: A user can direct disclosure through a custodian's online tool, or in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record. The priority order is: online tool first, then will, trust, or power of attorney, then the custodian's terms of service.
alabama.terms_of_service: A direction made through an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney overrides a contrary term in the custodian's terms of service. If the user left no direction at all, the terms of service govern, and the fiduciary then needs the user's consent in an estate document or a court order to reach the content of messages.
alabama.platform_tools: Google Inactive Account Manager lets a user name a trusted contact and set what happens after inactivity; Apple Legacy Contact lets a named person request access with a death certificate and an access key; Meta (Facebook and Instagram) lets a user name a legacy contact to manage a memorialized account or request removal. Each platform still requires its own form and proof of death, and a legacy-contact designation is treated as an online-tool direction.
alabama.what_to_do: 1. Make an inventory of accounts, devices, and crypto wallets. 2. Check each platform for an online-tool or legacy-contact designation. 3. Gather the will, trust, or power of attorney and the letters from the probate court. 4. Send each custodian a written request with a certified death certificate and proof of appointment. 5. If the custodian refuses or the content of messages is needed without consent, ask the probate court for an order.
alabama.agency_name: Alabama Attorney General, Consumer Interest Division
alabama.state_note: Alabama's act sits in Title 19 on fiduciaries rather than as a standalone technology law, and its custodian-disclosure section gives the custodian sole discretion to choose full access, partial access, or a copy of the assets.
alabama.sources: Ala. Code §§ 19-1A-1 through 19-1A-18 (Justia, 2025 Code of Alabama); Alabama HB 138, Act 2017-316; Alabama Attorney General Divisions page

delaware.rufada_status: Delaware has NOT adopted RUFADAA. It has its own earlier law, the Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets and Digital Accounts Act, HB 345, Chapter 416 (2014), signed August 12, 2014 and amended in 2025 (SB 143), codified at 12 Del. C. §§ 5001 through 5007.
delaware.custodian_access: A fiduciary, including a personal representative, guardian, agent under a durable power of attorney, or trustee, may exercise control over any and all rights in the account holder's digital assets and digital accounts, to the extent permitted by state or federal law or an end-user license agreement. The custodian must comply with a valid written request within 30 days. Delaware does not use RUFADAA's catalogue-versus-content split, so access turns on the governing instrument, the fiduciary's authority, and applicable privacy law rather than on a separate consent rule for message content.
delaware.user_direction: Delaware has no RUFADAA-style online-tool priority rule: the words online tool and designated recipient do not appear in Chapter 50. A user directs access mainly through a governing instrument such as a will, trust, or power of attorney that grants the fiduciary authority over digital assets, or through a court order. Platform tools such as Google Inactive Account Manager, Apple Legacy Contact, and Meta legacy contact still work as the platform's own settings, but Delaware law does not rank them above a will or trust the way RUFADAA does.
delaware.terms_of_service: A fiduciary's control is expressly subject to applicable state or federal law and to any end-user license agreement, so a custodian's terms can limit access in Delaware in a way RUFADAA's priority rule would not allow. If the user left no direction at all, the fiduciary's authority comes from the will, trust, or power of attorney and the court, and a custodian may still refuse disclosure that federal privacy law or its license terms forbid.
delaware.platform_tools: Google Inactive Account Manager lets a user name a trusted contact and set what happens after inactivity; Apple Legacy Contact lets a named person request access with a death certificate and an access key; Meta (Facebook and Instagram) lets a user name a legacy contact to manage a memorialized account or request removal. Each platform still requires its own form and proof of death. Because Delaware has no online-tool statute, these tools operate under the platform's own policy rather than under a state priority rule.
delaware.what_to_do: 1. Make an inventory of accounts, devices, and crypto wallets, including usernames and passwords, which Delaware's definition of digital asset expressly includes. 2. Check each platform for a legacy-contact or inactive-account designation. 3. Gather the will, trust, or durable power of attorney that grants digital-asset authority and the appointment from the Register of Wills. 4. Send each custodian a written request with a certified death certificate and proof of appointment. 5. If the custodian refuses, ask the Court of Chancery or the appropriate court for an order.
delaware.agency_name: Delaware Department of Justice, Fraud and Consumer Protection Division, Consumer Protection Unit
delaware.state_note: Delaware was the first state in the nation to pass a digital-assets access law in 2014, a year before the Uniform Law Commission finished RUFADAA, and it kept its own broader law instead of adopting RUFADAA. Its definition of digital asset expressly includes usernames and passwords.
delaware.sources: 12 Del. C. §§ 5001 through 5007 (Delaware Code); Delaware HB 345, 79 Del. Laws, Chapter 416, signed August 12, 2014 (Delaware General Assembly); Delaware Department of Justice homepage

hawaii.rufada_status: Adopted RUFADAA. Hawaii enacted the Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (2015) as SB 2298 in 2016, effective July 1, 2016, codified at Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 556A.
hawaii.custodian_access: A fiduciary such as a personal representative, trustee, agent under a power of attorney, or conservator can get a catalogue of electronic communications (who the user communicated with, when, and at what address) and other digital assets such as photos, files, and online accounts. The content of electronic communications, such as the text of emails and messages, is disclosed only if the user consented through an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney, or if a court orders it. The custodian must comply within 60 days after receiving the required proof and may ask for a written request, a certified death certificate, letters of appointment, an account identifier, and evidence of the user's consent.
hawaii.user_direction: The user can direct disclosure through the custodian's online tool, such as Google Inactive Account Manager or a legacy contact, or in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record. Priority order is: first, a direction made through an online tool that the user can change at any time; second, a direction in a will, trust, or power of attorney; third, the custodian's terms of service.
hawaii.terms_of_service: A user's direction made through an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney overrides a contrary term in the custodian's terms of service, unless that term required the user to act affirmatively and distinctly from simply agreeing to the terms. If the user left no direction, the custodian's terms of service govern, and the default rules then apply: the fiduciary can get the catalogue and other digital assets, but not the content of communications without consent or a court order.
hawaii.platform_tools: Google Inactive Account Manager lets the user name trusted contacts and set what happens after inactivity. Apple Legacy Contact lets the user name a person who can request access with an access key and a death certificate. Meta (Facebook and Instagram) offers a legacy contact and memorialization, and requires proof of death and proof of authority. Each platform still applies its own process on top of Hawaii law.
hawaii.what_to_do: First, inventory the accounts, devices, passwords, and crypto wallets. Second, check whether the user set up an online tool or legacy contact. Third, gather the will, trust, or power of attorney and the letters of appointment. Fourth, send each custodian a written request with a certified death certificate and the appointment papers. Fifth, if the custodian refuses or the content is needed, ask the circuit court for an order.
hawaii.state_statute: Haw. Rev. Stat. ch. 556A, sections 556A-1 et seq.
hawaii.agency_name: Hawaii Department of the Attorney General
hawaii.state_note: Hawaii placed the act in its own chapter, Chapter 556A, rather than inside its probate code, and the act applies only if the user resided in Hawaii at death.
hawaii.sources: Hawaii Legislature, SB 2298 (2016), Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act; Hawaii Commission to Promote Uniform Legislation testimony, February 13, 2019, stating the act is now Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 556A; Uniform Law Commission, Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (2015) summary

idaho.rufada_status: Adopted RUFADAA. Idaho enacted the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act in 2016 (Senate Bill 1303, chapter 263), effective July 1, 2016, codified at Idaho Code Title 15, Chapter 14.
idaho.custodian_access: A personal representative, trustee, agent, conservator, or guardian can get a catalogue of electronic communications and other digital assets, such as files, photos, and account records. The content of electronic communications is disclosed only if the user consented or a court orders it. The custodian must comply within 60 days after receiving the required information and may ask for a written request, a certified death certificate, a certified copy of the letters of appointment or a small estate affidavit or court order, an account identifier, and evidence of consent. The custodian may grant full access, partial access, or a copy, and may charge a reasonable administrative fee.
idaho.user_direction: The user can direct disclosure through the custodian's online tool, or in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record. Priority order is: first, an online-tool direction the user can modify or delete at any time, which overrides a contrary direction in a will or trust; second, a direction in a will, trust, or power of attorney; third, the custodian's terms of service.
idaho.terms_of_service: A user's direction through an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney overrides a contrary term of service that did not require the user to act affirmatively and distinctly from assenting to the terms. If the user left no direction, the terms of service govern first, and the act's default rules then apply: the fiduciary can get the catalogue and other assets, but not message content without consent or a court order.
idaho.platform_tools: Google Inactive Account Manager, Apple Legacy Contact, and Meta legacy contact and memorialization all apply. Apple requires the legacy contact's access key and a death certificate. Meta requires proof of death and proof of authority, and may memorialize the account or remove it. Google follows the user's Inactive Account Manager choice where one was set.

illinois.rufada_status: Adopted RUFADAA. Illinois enacted the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (2015) as Public Act 99-775, signed August 12, 2016 and effective that day, codified at 755 ILCS 70.
illinois.custodian_access: A personal representative, guardian, agent, or trustee can get a catalogue of electronic communications and other digital assets, such as photos, documents, and online accounts. The content of electronic communications is disclosed only if the user consented through an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney, or if a court orders it. The custodian must comply no later than 60 days after receiving the required information and may ask for a written request, a certified death certificate, letters of appointment, an account identifier, and evidence of the user's consent. The custodian may grant full access, partial access, or a copy of the assets.
illinois.user_direction: The user can direct disclosure through the custodian's online tool, or in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record. Priority order is: first, an online-tool direction the user can modify or delete at any time; second, a direction in a will, trust, or power of attorney; third, the custodian's terms of service.
illinois.terms_of_service: A user's direction through an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney overrides a contrary term of service that did not require the user to act affirmatively and distinctly from assenting to the terms. If the user left no direction, the terms of service govern, and the act's default rules then apply: the fiduciary can get the catalogue and other assets, but not the content of communications without consent or a court order.

Google follows the user's Inactive Account Manager choice where one was set.

louisiana.rufada_status: Has NOT adopted RUFADAA. Louisiana is one of the few states that never enacted it. House Bill 1118 in the 2016 Regular Session would have enacted RUFADAA as Revised Statutes sections 51:2701 to 51:2720; it passed the House and Senate in different forms but died in conference and was never signed. Instead, Louisiana has its own narrower 2014 law, Code of Civil Procedure Article 3191, paragraphs C through H, added by Acts 2014, Number 758.
louisiana.custodian_access: Under Article 3191, a succession representative (the executor or administrator, called a succession representative in Louisiana) has power to take control of, handle, continue, distribute, or terminate any digital account of the decedent, subject to any restriction in a valid testament or a court order. The holder of the account must transfer, deliver, or provide access or possession within 30 days after receiving the letters testamentary, letters of administration, or letters of independent administration, to the extent federal law permits. Federally insured financial institutions follow Revised Statutes sections 6:325 and 6:767 instead. The article covers only a succession representative; it has no equivalent provision for an agent under a power of attorney, a trustee, or a curator.
louisiana.user_direction: Louisiana has no RUFADAA priority order, so there is no statute ranking an online tool first, then a will or trust, then terms of service. In practice, use the platform's own tool first, such as Google Inactive Account Manager or Apple Legacy Contact or a Meta legacy contact, because the platform controls its own account. Then look to the decedent's testament for any restriction on the succession representative's power, since Article 3191(C) makes the representative's power subject to a restriction in a valid testament or a court order. A person planning ahead should also name a mandatary under a mandate and leave clear written instructions, since Article 3191 does not cover incapacity.
louisiana.terms_of_service: Article 3191(E) expressly supersedes any contrary provision in a service agreement, and treats the succession representative as an authorized user with the decedent's lawful consent for purposes of accessing or possessing the digital accounts. That is stronger than RUFADAA on this point. Even so, the duty applies only to the extent permitted by federal law, and the federal Stored Communications Act still limits when a provider may disclose the contents of electronic communications.
louisiana.platform_tools: Google Inactive Account Manager, Apple Legacy Contact, and Meta legacy contact and memorialization all apply as the practical first route, since Louisiana has no statute ranking them. Apple requires the legacy contact's access key and a death certificate. Meta requires proof of death and proof of authority, and may memorialize the account or remove it. Google follows the user's Inactive Account Manager choice where one was set.
louisiana.what_to_do: First, inventory the accounts, devices, and crypto. Second, check whether the user set up an online tool or legacy contact and follow that route first. Third, open the succession in district court and get letters testamentary, letters of administration, or letters of independent administration. Fourth, send each account holder a written request with the letters and a certified death certificate, and note the 30-day duty in Article 3191. Fifth, if the holder refuses, ask the district court to enforce the article or order access, and get legal advice on the federal Stored Communications Act if message content is at issue.
louisiana.state_statute: La. Code Civ. P. art. 3191, paragraphs C to H (Acts 2014, No. 758; amended by Acts 2023, No. 38, effective July 1, 2023); see also La. Rev. Stat. sections 6:325 and 6:767 for financial institutions
louisiana.agency_name: Louisiana Attorney General, Consumer Protection Section
louisiana.state_note: Louisiana is the only state in this set that never adopted RUFADAA, and its substitute law has no catalogue-versus-content split: Article 3191 defines a digital account to include the text, images, and multimedia stored through it, but the 30-day duty still applies only to the extent federal law permits.

massachusetts.rufada_status: Massachusetts has NOT adopted RUFADAA. No digital-assets act exists in the Massachusetts General Laws, and the probate code (M.G.L. c. 190B) has no digital-assets article. Bills to adopt it in the 194th General Court were reported favorably in 2025-2026 but have not been enacted. Massachusetts is one of only three states that have not adopted RUFADAA.
massachusetts.custodian_access: There is no Massachusetts statute forcing a custodian to disclose an account to a fiduciary. A personal representative's authority comes only from the general probate duty to take possession of the decedent's property (M.G.L. c. 190B, section 3-709) and to inventory it (section 3-706), which runs to the property, not to the provider. In practice the custodian decides under its own terms of service, and the federal Stored Communications Act generally bars a provider from disclosing the contents of emails and messages without the user's consent or a court order. There is no statutory 60-day deadline for a custodian to respond.
massachusetts.user_direction: Because there is no state statute, the user's own planning does all the work: set up each platform's online tool (Google Inactive Account Manager, Apple Legacy Contact, Meta legacy contact), and put express digital-asset authority in the will, trust, or durable power of attorney, naming who may access which accounts. Without a statute there is no legally fixed priority order, so the platform's tool and the written documents should agree with each other.
massachusetts.terms_of_service: Yes — in Massachusetts the custodian's terms of service effectively control, since no state law overrides them. If the user left no direction, the family must ask the custodian under its deceased-user process, and the custodian may refuse, delete, or memorialize the account as its terms allow. A probate court order can sometimes compel access, but there is no statute guaranteeing it.
massachusetts.platform_tools: Google Inactive Account Manager lets the user name a trusted contact who gets access or deletion after a set period of inactivity; Apple Legacy Contact lets a designated person request access with an access key and death certificate; Meta (Facebook and Instagram) offers a legacy contact or memorialization, and requires a death certificate and proof of authority for removal or access. Each platform has its own request form and proof requirements.
massachusetts.what_to_do: 1. Inventory every account, device, password manager, and crypto wallet, including any seed phrases stored at home. 2. Check whether the person set up Google Inactive Account Manager, an Apple Legacy Contact, or a Meta legacy contact. 3. Gather the will, trust, or power of attorney and the letters of appointment from the Probate and Family Court. 4. Contact each custodian with a death certificate and proof of authority and follow its deceased-user process. 5. If a custodian refuses access to message content, ask a probate attorney about a court order, since there is no statute to rely on.
massachusetts.state_statute: No RUFADAA statute. General probate authority only: M.G.L. c. 190B, sections 3-706 and 3-709.
massachusetts.agency_name: Massachusetts Attorney General, Consumer Advocacy and Response Division
massachusetts.state_note: Massachusetts is one of only three states that still has no RUFADAA law at all, so families here depend entirely on platform tools and careful estate documents.
massachusetts.sources: Settled Estate, Massachusetts Digital Assets After Death (July 2026) — https://www.settledestate.com/massachusetts/digital-assets/; Massachusetts Legislature, bill text for H.1968/S.1048 (194th General Court) — https://malegislature.gov/Bills/194/H1968.pdf; ProbatePedia, RUFADAA state adoption list (March 2026) — https://www.probatepedia.com/digital-accounts-after-death/rufadaa-digital-asset-law-executor-access/; Massachusetts Attorney General consumer services — https://www.mass.gov/info-details/consumer-services-at-the-attorney-generals-office

michigan.rufada_status: Michigan adopted its version of the act in 2016 as the Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, Act 59 of 2016, effective June 27, 2016, codified at MCL sections 700.1001 and following.
michigan.custodian_access: A fiduciary (personal representative, conservator, agent, or trustee) can get a catalogue of electronic communications — who the user communicated with, when, and at what address — and other digital assets such as photos, files, and online accounts. The content of emails and messages is disclosed only if the user consented or a court orders it. The custodian may grant full access, partial access, or a copy of the assets, and may demand a written request, a death certificate, proof of fiduciary authority, and the account identifier. The custodian must comply within 60 days of receiving the required documents, and a fiduciary who is refused can ask the court for an order compelling disclosure.
michigan.user_direction: The user can direct disclosure through the custodian's online tool, or in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other written record. Under Michigan's act, a direction made through an online tool that can be changed or deleted at any time overrides a contrary direction in a will, trust, or power of attorney. If no online tool was used, the will, trust, or power of attorney controls, and either user direction overrides a contrary term in the custodian's terms of service.
michigan.terms_of_service: The terms of service cannot override the user's direction given through an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney. If the user left no direction at all, the terms of service may modify or eliminate the fiduciary's access, and the act's default rules apply — the fiduciary gets the catalogue and other digital assets, but not message content without consent or a court order.

minnesota.rufada_status: Minnesota adopted the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act in 2016 (2016 c. 135), signed May 22, 2016, effective August 1, 2016, codified at Minnesota Statutes Chapter 521A.
minnesota.custodian_access: A fiduciary (personal representative, conservator, agent, or trustee) can get a catalogue of electronic communications — who the user communicated with, when, and at what address — and other digital assets such as photos, files, and online accounts. The custodian may grant full access, partial access, or a copy of the assets, and may demand a written request, a death certificate, proof of fiduciary authority, and the account identifier. new mexico.rufada_status: Yes. New Mexico adopted the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act in 2017 (Senate Bill 60, Laws 2017, chapter 72), effective January 1, 2018. It is codified at NMSA 1978, Sections 46-13-1 through 46-13-18.
new mexico.custodian_access: A fiduciary can get a catalogue of electronic communications (who sent and received messages, and when) and other digital assets such as photos and files, by giving the custodian a written request, a certified death certificate, letters testamentary or of administration, the account identifier, and evidence linking the account to the user. The content of emails and other private messages is disclosed only if the user consented or a court orders it. The custodian must comply within 60 days of receiving the required proof, may grant full or partial access or provide a copy, and may charge a reasonable administrative fee.
new mexico.user_direction: The user can direct disclosure through the custodian's online tool, such as Google Inactive Account Manager or Apple Legacy Contact, or in a will, trust, or power of attorney. The online tool controls first; if there is no online-tool direction, the will, trust, or power of attorney controls; if there is no direction at all, the custodian's terms of service control.
new mexico.terms_of_service: The terms of service cannot override a direction the user gave through an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney. If the user left no direction, the terms of service can limit or eliminate the fiduciary's access.
new mexico.platform_tools: Google Inactive Account Manager lets the user name a trusted contact and choose whether the account is shared or deleted after inactivity. Apple Legacy Contact lets a named person request access to the user's Apple data with a death certificate and an access key. oklahoma.rufada_status: No. Oklahoma has NOT adopted RUFADAA. Two independent sources confirm this: ProbatePedia's 2026 state-by-state table lists Oklahoma among the three states that have not adopted RUFADAA, and Law Commentary, citing the National Conference of State Legislatures, likewise names Oklahoma as a holdout, noting a RUFADAA bill has sat in the House Rules Committee since February 2020. The only state law is a narrow 2010 statute, Okla. Stat. tit. 58, Section 269, letting an executor or administrator take control of a deceased person's social networking, microblogging, and email accounts.
oklahoma.custodian_access: There is no Oklahoma statute setting out the RUFADAA catalogue-versus-content rules or a 60-day deadline. Under the 2010 law, an executor or administrator may take control of, continue, or terminate the decedent's social networking, microblogging, and email accounts where otherwise authorized. For anything beyond that, access depends on the custodian's own policies, the user's own directions, and general probate law, and a court order is the usual fallback when a custodian refuses.
oklahoma.user_direction: Because Oklahoma has no RUFADAA priority ladder, there is no state-law rule that an online tool beats a will or that a will beats the terms of service. In practice, the platform's own tools still matter most: Google Inactive Account Manager, Apple Legacy Contact, and Meta's legacy contact let the user name someone in advance, and a will or power of attorney that expressly grants digital-asset authority strengthens the fiduciary's request to the custodian.
oklahoma.terms_of_service: Without RUFADAA, the custodian's terms of service carry much more weight in Oklahoma than in the other states in this batch. If the user left no direction, the terms of service and the custodian's deceased-user policy generally decide what, if anything, the family can get, unless a court orders disclosure.

Apple Legacy Contact lets a named person request access to the user's Apple data with a death certificate and an access key. Meta lets a Facebook user name a legacy contact to manage a memorialized account, and Instagram memorializes accounts on request with proof of death. Because Oklahoma has no RUFADAA, these platform tools are the most reliable way to arrange access in advance.
oklahoma.what_to_do: 1. Make an inventory of the person's accounts, devices, and passwords. 2. Check whether the person named anyone through an online tool such as Google Inactive Account Manager or Apple Legacy Contact. 3. Gather the will and the death certificate, and get appointed as executor or administrator. 4. Contact each custodian with the death certificate and proof of appointment, citing the 2010 statute for social media and email accounts. 5. south dakota.platform_tools: Google Inactive Account Manager lets the user name up to ten trusted contacts and choose which data they receive after a chosen period of inactivity. Apple Legacy Contact lets the user name contacts who can request iCloud data with an access key and a death certificate. Meta (Facebook and Instagram) lets the user name a legacy contact to manage a memorialized profile, or choose deletion on death; the legacy contact cannot log in as the user or read private messages.
south dakota.what_to_do: First, make an inventory of accounts, devices, and crypto wallets and keys. Second, check whether the person set up an online tool such as Google Inactive Account Manager, Apple Legacy Contact, or a Meta legacy contact. Third, gather the will, trust, or power of attorney that names the fiduciary and gives digital-asset authority. Fourth, send each custodian a written request with a death certificate and proof of appointment. Fifth, if the custodian refuses or does not answer within 60 days, ask the probate court for an order directing disclosure.

The content of electronic communications is disclosed only if the user consented to it in an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney, or if a court orders it. The custodian must comply within 60 days after receiving the required proof, may give full access, partial access, or a copy of the records, and may charge a reasonable administrative fee. It may require a written request, a death certificate, letters of appointment, a copy of the will, trust, or power of attorney, and an account identifier or evidence linking the account to the user.
wyoming.user_direction: The user can direct disclosure through a custodian's online tool, naming a designated recipient, and can also allow or forbid disclosure in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record. The priority order is: first the online tool, then the will, trust, or power of attorney, then the custodian's terms of service.
wyoming.terms_of_service: The custodian's terms of service cannot override a direction the user gave through an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney. If the user left no direction, the terms of service can limit or eliminate the fiduciary's access, and the fiduciary then gets only what the statute allows without the user's consent to content.
wyoming.platform_tools: Google Inactive Account Manager lets the user name up to ten trusted contacts and choose which data they receive after a chosen period of inactivity. Apple Legacy Contact lets the user name contacts who can request iCloud data with an access key and a death certificate. Meta (Facebook and Instagram) lets the user name a legacy contact to manage a memorialized profile, or choose deletion on death; the legacy contact cannot log in as the user or read private messages.
wyoming.what_to_do: First, make an inventory of accounts, devices, and crypto wallets and keys. Second, check whether the person set up an online tool such as Google Inactive Account Manager, Apple Legacy Contact, or a Meta legacy contact. Third, gather the will, trust, or power of attorney that names the fiduciary and gives digital-asset authority. Fourth, send each custodian a written request with a death certificate and proof of appointment. Fifth, if the custodian refuses or does not answer within 60 days, ask the probate court for an order directing disclosure.
wyoming.agency_name: Wyoming Attorney General, Consumer Protection and Antitrust Unit
wyoming.state_note: Wyoming was one of the first three states to adopt the uniform act, in March 2016, and it later adopted separate laws on digital assets such as cryptocurrency, which are different from this fiduciary-access law and do not replace it.
